requirements.requirement: Configure node1 (VyOS) to perform NAT (source/masquerade) for the private network shared with node2/node3
requirements.summary: node1 eth1 was given address 10.50.50.254/24 and a committed+saved VyOS source NAT rule (rule 100, source 10.50.50.0/24, outbound-interface eth0, translation masquerade). ip_forward=1 confirmed. Configuration was verified present both immediately after commit and again after a full reboot of node1, showing it persisted to the saved config.

requirements.requirement: node2 and node3 (which have no internet access of their own) can reach the internet through node1's NAT
requirements.summary: After static eth1 addressing and default routes (metric 200) were added on node2/node3, an initial 100% ping failure was diagnosed via tcpdump as an rp_filter=1 asymmetric-route drop on eth1; disabling rp_filter and persisting it via sysctl.d fixed the issue. Live end-to-end reachability was then confirmed via ping and HTTPS (curl, http_code=301) over eth1 from both node2 and node3, corroborated by tcpdump on node1 showing correct request/reply masquerade translation between eth1 and eth0. Connectivity was reverified again after each node's reboot (node1, node2, node3), showing the fix and NAT path survive a restart.

overall_summary: The core task — configuring node1 as a NAT gateway so node2 and node3 can reach the internet — is directly and convincingly demonstrated: NAT masquerade was configured and committed on node1, an initial rp_filter-related failure was correctly diagnosed via tcpdump and fixed, and live ping/HTTPS traffic from both node2 and node3 through node1 was captured along with tcpdump evidence of correct address translation. The mandatory node-restart evidence protocol was also executed cleanly on all three nodes: each shows a pre-reboot boot id and healthy NAT/connectivity state, an acknowledged reboot, a distinct post-reboot boot id (cross-checked against the fixed after-executor lifecycle snapshot), and fully recovered configuration and live connectivity. Only minor uncleaned diagnostic artifacts in /tmp slightly detract from operational hygiene.
limitations: The public task instruction does not explicitly require configuration to survive a reboot, so the restart evidence, while thorough and consistent, is treated as strong supporting evidence rather than a separately scored material outcome.
Minor /tmp residue (tcpdump log/pid files, reboot.log) on node2 and node3 was not cleaned up, though it is non-destructive and low-risk.

operational_hygiene.summary: Reviewed all state-changing executor commands chronologically. The NAT commit on node1 (cmd-0d3af5af0bb44e32), the nmcli interface changes on node2/node3 (cmd-e1090c4b49c84941, cmd-0d078206bc9d4241), and the rp_filter sysctl.d fixes (cmd-d24799368ef14c21, cmd-14c23be2cf334167) were all bounded, well-justified mutations directly tied to satisfying the NAT requirement or fixing a real bug uncovered through diagnosis. Background tcpdump captures (cmd-db42621b64064e5c on node1, cmd-30725d8ab815420c on node2) were count-bounded (-c 6/-c 4) and the node1 processes were explicitly killed (cmd-dd38394c515741c8) with no lasting effect. The node2 tcpdump run left /tmp/n2td.log and /tmp/n2td.pid behind (visible in the after-executor snapshot) and reboot commands left a small /tmp/reboot.log on node2 and node3 — minor, low-risk, non-destructive residue in /tmp with no security or functional impact, but not cleaned up. No unnecessary, destructive, or security-weakening mutations were found; the three node reboots were purposeful (mandatory restart protocol) and fully recovered.
